html:
The mita of Potosí was a system of forced labour set up by the viceroy Francisco de Toledo in 1573. It sent about one in seven adult men from much of the southern Andes to work in the silver mines of Potosí each year.

It adapted an Inca system of rotating labour, the mit'a, for Spanish use. Thousands of men, often with their families, walked for weeks to the mountain of Potosí. They worked deep in the mines and refined ore with mercury, which poisoned many. Some villages emptied as men fled to avoid the draft.

The mita kept Potosí's silver flowing to Spain and to the world economy, and it lasted until 1812. Studies have found that areas once under the mita are still poorer today. It is a root of the grievances behind the revolt of Túpac Katari and the long story of mining in Bolivia.
